Frontier models now acquire most of their breadth from reinforcement learning on many domains at once. A single policy is trained on competition math, instruction following, tool use, search, terminal work and software-engineering episodes, with one optimizer and batches that mix rollouts from all of them. The mixed batch rests on an assumption that is rarely stated: the domains’ updates can simply be added. At every step, what happens to a domain is its own gradient plus whatever the other domains’ gradients do to it.

When domains agree, that second term is free transfer. When they conflict, it is a tax, and it falls on the domains least able to pay: those with a small share of the batch, small gradients, or episodes slow enough that the run moves on without them. The usual remedies each trade this problem for another. Training domains in sequence forgets the earlier ones. Training specialists apart and merging their weights once lands tens to hundreds of nats from every policy that produced data ,. Distilling the specialists into one student with multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD), the recipe in recent frontier reports ,,, needs a second round of rollouts in every domain and at best matches its teachers.

Our starting point is a merge rule, not a training loop. Let trainers move from a shared anchor θˉ\bar\thetaθˉ by updates Δi\Delta_iΔi​. The model whose behaviour on each domain is closest in KL to that domain’s trainer has, to second order, a closed form, a Fisher-weighted average θ+=θˉ+(∑iFi)+∑iFiΔi\theta^{+}=\bar\theta+\big(\sum_iF_i\big)^{+}\sum_iF_i\Delta_iθ+=θˉ+(∑i​Fi​)+∑i​Fi​Δi​, and the choice of Fisher is what does the work. With FiF_iFi​ taken on trainer iii’s own on-policy rollouts, its policy gradient lies in the range of FiF_iFi​: a change that domain’s Fisher cannot see is a change its return cannot feel. Whenever the trainers’ updates can be reconciled, the merged model therefore keeps every domain’s own first-order gain and drops every cross-domain term.

The rule is accurate only locally. It is a second-order expansion around each trainer, and its weights are each trainer’s current Fisher, which fades on exactly the behaviour a trainer has become confident about. Applied once to finished specialists, tens to hundreds of nats apart, it still works: merging five released 4B RL specialists with no training and no student rollouts beats task arithmetic by 1.3 points and the released MOPD model by 0.8 points on a domain-balanced benchmark mean. But it leaves part of each specialist behind, and nothing corrects what it misses.

On-Policy Merge (OPM) therefore applies the rule during training, keeping the specialists’ independence and giving up only the distance. Each domain has its own on-policy trainer, started from a shared anchor. As soon as any trainer has drifted a fixed KL budget δ\deltaδ from the anchor, all of them merge with the rule above, measured on the rollouts each trainer has just collected. Every trainer reloads the merged model and continues, and the next round of RL repairs what the merge missed. Train apart, meet often: often enough that every merge stays where the rule is accurate.

This is the sense in which OPM stabilizes multi-task RL. Each domain improves whenever its own trainer does, whatever the batch shares, gradient scales or speeds of the others, and a domain that stalls or breaks is held in place rather than dragged. Decoupling removes transfer of both signs, so OPM is not a faster optimizer: when domains help each other, summing their updates does better, and at the same bf16 precision plain summation beats the one-shot merge by 0.6, as the theory predicts for math, science and code. What OPM buys is a per-domain guarantee at a measurable price: one model copy per domain, and a merge that takes about ten minutes on a 9B model with a guarded solver and needs no environment interaction.

The rest of the post places OPM among the existing recipes, derives the merge, why it must be applied often and what it guarantees, shows how to make it cheap, and tests it: first on those released specialists, then against strong multi-task RL, merging after training and MOPD on eight frontier-style domains at 9B. The 9B results are marked as pending until the runs finish.

#Five ways to get one model

Every method for combining RL domains makes two choices: how often the domains’ progress is combined, and by what rule. Figure 1 shows the first choice, and Table 1 sets both side by side.

Multi-task RL combines at every step, in parameter space: one optimizer receives the sum of the domains’ gradients, weighted by their token shares in the batch. With plain SGD this is exactly the same as running one trainer per domain and summing their updates after every step (Appendix A). Combining every KKK steps instead gives periodic summing or averaging, the federated-averaging and DiLoCo family ,. Combining once, after training, gives merge-after methods: task arithmetic, TIES and DARE ,,. Cascade RL trains the domains one after another ,. In these terms it is multi-task RL with every share but one set to zero, which is why nothing holds the other domains in place while one trains.

MOPD changes the geometry instead of the frequency. The student minimises the sum of reverse KLs to the teachers on its own rollouts, and to second order this solves a Fisher-weighted merge , with the Fisher measured on the student’s states and paid for with fresh rollouts in every domain. Distral and Divide-and-Conquer RL use the same KL barycenter as their shared policy and reach it by distillation ,.

OPM takes the remaining combination. It combines during training, as often as a KL budget demands, in KL geometry, with the Fisher measured on each trainer’s own states. Table 1 lists what each method pays.

MethodHow oftenGeometryReward when combiningWhat it pays
Multi-task RLEvery stepEuclidean, one shared optimizerYesDomains interfere through the shared step; weak or slow domains lose their share.
Periodic sum or averageEvery KKK stepsEuclideanYesThe sum presumes no domain sees another’s update; the average presumes every domain sees every update equally.
Merge-after (TA, TIES, DARE)OnceEuclideanNoThe merged model is far from every policy that produced data, and pays for the whole drift at once.
MOPDOnce, then a distillation stageKL, student statesNo, unless an outcome reward is addedA second rollout stage in every domain; capped at the teachers.
OPMWhen a trainer’s KL reaches δ\deltaδKL, trainer statesYes, in every local stepRemoves positive transfer along with interference; one model copy per domain.

Table 1. How often each method combines the domains, in which geometry, whether reward is used when combining, and what it pays.

The rules are related exactly, not by analogy (Appendix A,Table A2). Summing is OPM when the domains’ Fishers are mutually orthogonal. Averaging is OPM when they are all equal. With one natural-gradient step per trainer, the OPM merge is a natural policy gradient step on the summed objective . Task arithmetic with a coefficient between 1/n1/n1/n and 1 interpolates between the presumptions of the average and the sum (Table 1). OPM measures, direction by direction, which one holds; Figure 2 shows what that looks like in weight space.

#On-Policy Merge

This section builds OPM step by step: what a merge of RL trainers should preserve, the closed form that preserves it, the Fisher that makes the closed form right for RL, why the merge has to happen during training, and the loop that runs it.

What a merge should preserve. Each trainer has learned something about its own domain, and the merged model should keep it. We measure that by behaviour, not by weights: on domain iii, the merged model’s rollouts should look like trainer iii’s. A rollout ξ=(h1,a1,…,hL,aL)\xi=(h_1,a_1,\dots,h_L,a_L)ξ=(h1​,a1​,…,hL​,aL​) has probability Pθi(ξ)=∏tπθ(at∣ht)P^i_\theta(\xi)=\prod_t\pi_\theta(a_t\mid h_t)Pθi​(ξ)=∏t​πθ​(at​∣ht​) times environment terms that do not depend on θ\thetaθ, so the KL between rollout distributions is well defined and the environment cancels from it. The merge we want is the KL barycenter of the trainers:

θ+∈arg⁡min⁡θ  ∑iKL(Pθii ∥ Pθi).(1)\theta^{+}\in\arg\min_\theta\;\sum_i\mathrm{KL}\big(P^i_{\theta_i}\,\|\,P^i_\theta\big).\tag{1}θ+∈argθmin​i∑​KL(Pθi​i​∥Pθi​).(1)

Up to a constant, (1) is the negative log-likelihood of every trainer’s own rollouts under the merged model, so it needs nothing the trainers do not already hold. The objective is not new: Distral and Divide-and-Conquer RL use it for their shared policy and reach it by distillation ,. What is new is solving it in closed form, in one shared network, during training.

The closed form. Let trainer iii move from the anchor to θi=θˉ+Δi\theta_i=\bar\theta+\Delta_iθi​=θˉ+Δi​. Expanding each KL to second order around its trainer, KL≈12(θ−θi)⊤Fi(θ−θi)\mathrm{KL}\approx\tfrac12(\theta-\theta_i)^\top F_i(\theta-\theta_i)KL≈21​(θ−θi​)⊤Fi​(θ−θi​), and setting the gradient of the sum to zero gives the OPM merge:

  θ+=θˉ+(∑iFi)+∑iFi Δi  ,Fi=Eξ∼Pθii[∑tstst⊤],st=∇log⁡πθi(at∣ht).(2)\boxed{\;\theta^{+}=\bar\theta+\Big(\sum_iF_i\Big)^{+}\sum_iF_i\,\Delta_i\;},\qquad F_i=\mathbb{E}_{\xi\sim P^i_{\theta_i}}\Big[\sum_t s_ts_t^\top\Big],\quad s_t=\nabla\log\pi_{\theta_i}(a_t\mid h_t).\tag{2}θ+=θˉ+(i∑​Fi​)+i∑​Fi​Δi​​,Fi​=Eξ∼Pθi​i​​[t∑​st​st⊤​],st​=∇logπθi​​(at​∣ht​).(2)

Read (2) one direction of weight space at a time. Where only domain iii has curvature, the anchor takes all of Δi\Delta_iΔi​. Where several domains do, it takes their curvature-weighted mean. Where none does, it moves nowhere any domain can see. For tabular policies the exact minimiser of (1) is, at every history, the mixture of the trainers’ action distributions weighted by how often each visits it; (2) is its second-order version.

Which Fisher. Formula (2) is Fisher-weighted averaging , and everything depends on which Fisher. OPM uses the on-policy Fisher: the Fisher of trainer iii’s current policy on its own domain, estimated from rollouts that policy has just sampled and summed over the tokens of each rollout. One property makes this the right choice for RL. Write S(ξ)=∑tstS(\xi)=\sum_ts_tS(ξ)=∑t​st​ for the score of a rollout and bbb for any reward baseline. For every direction vvv,

Fiv=0  ⟹  E[(v⊤S)2]=0  ⟹  v⊤S=0 on every rollout  ⟹  v⊤∇Ji=E[(Ri−b) v⊤S]=0.F_iv=0\;\Longrightarrow\;\mathbb{E}\big[(v^\top S)^2\big]=0\;\Longrightarrow\;v^\top S=0\ \text{on every rollout}\;\Longrightarrow\;v^\top\nabla J_i=\mathbb{E}\big[(R_i-b)\,v^\top S\big]=0 .Fi​v=0⟹E[(v⊤S)2]=0⟹v⊤S=0 on every rollout⟹v⊤∇Ji​=E[(Ri​−b)v⊤S]=0.

The policy gradient lies in the range of the on-policy Fisher: a change that a domain’s Fisher cannot see is a change its return cannot feel. That is why a merge that respects each Fisher can respect each return without ever looking at a reward. The argument needs the gradient and the Fisher to be expectations under the same distribution. It fails for the empirical Fisher of stale or foreign rollouts, a different and biased object , and for supervised gradients against a model Fisher. Hence the name: the data, the metric and, as the loop below ensures, the continuation are all on-policy.

Why meet often. Formula (2) is a second-order expansion with weights measured at the trainers, so it is accurate only locally. Four things degrade as the trainers drift apart, and each is a reason to merge during training rather than after it.

  • Locality. The cubic remainder of the quadratic model accumulates token by token; over a run of RRR rounds its total falls as 1/R21/R^21/R2 (Appendix B.4). In a two-action example the locality ratio κ\kappaκ, true KL over its quadratic prediction, grows from 1.00 to 1.92 after 20 steps and to 8.9 after 200.
  • Calibration. As a trainer grows confident, its Fisher vanishes on the logits it pushed, so a late merge undervalues exactly what the trainer learned best.
  • Repair. After a merge during training, the next round of RL starts from the merged model and corrects with reward what the merge missed. A merge after training has no second chance.
  • Continuation. A merge that moves each trainer by a small per-token KL keeps its rollouts in flight usable under per-token importance weights, so training never stops for a hand-over.

Frequency does not fix everything. Where domains genuinely conflict, each round leaves a second-order residual whose first-order reward cost does not shrink with frequency, and where the domains’ Fishers do not overlap, frequency changes nothing. How often to merge is therefore a trade-off against the cost of a merge, which the engineering section makes small and the frequency sweep measures.

The loop. OPM runs one ordinary on-policy trainer per domain from a shared anchor and merges them by (2) whenever the drift of any trainer from the anchor, Di=KL(Pθii ∥ Pθˉi)D_i=\mathrm{KL}(P^i_{\theta_i}\,\|\,P^i_{\bar\theta})Di​=KL(Pθi​i​∥Pθˉi​), reaches its ceiling δi\delta_iδi​. We call each merge a rendezvous. The drift is measured on a subsample of each batch and never penalised. Algorithm 1 gives the whole procedure.

#What the merge guarantees, and what it costs

The property above says that (2) never moves a domain’s return through a direction its Fisher ignores. This section asks what the merge guarantees in the directions that remain, what multi-task RL lacks by comparison, and what the guarantee costs. Each statement carries a status in Appendix B (theorem, proposition under stated assumptions, or conjecture with numerical support), with its proof.

When a merge loses nothing. Each domain’s policy is unchanged, to second order, along the affine subspace θj+null⁡(Fj)\theta_j+\operatorname{null}(F_j)θj​+null(Fj​): a flat-bottomed trough in weight space (Figure 2). Call a round lossless if the troughs meet, that is, if some displacement ddd satisfies Fj(d−Δj)=0F_j(d-\Delta_j)=0Fj​(d−Δj​)=0 for every jjj. This holds for every possible set of updates exactly when the Fisher ranges are linearly independent: independent, not orthogonal.

Theorem 1 · decoupling

In a lossless round, (2) returns a lossless point and, for every domain jjj, to first order in the displacements,

Jj(θ+)−Jj(θj)=0,Jj(θˉ+∑iΔi)−Jj(θ+)=Tj,Tj=∇Jj(θj)⊤∑i≠jΔi.J_j(\theta^{+})-J_j(\theta_j)=0,\qquad J_j\Big(\bar\theta+\sum_i\Delta_i\Big)-J_j(\theta^{+})=T_j,\qquad T_j=\nabla J_j(\theta_j)^\top\sum_{i\ne j}\Delta_i .Jj​(θ+)−Jj​(θj​)=0,Jj​(θˉ+i∑​Δi​)−Jj​(θ+)=Tj​,Tj​=∇Jj​(θj​)⊤i=j∑​Δi​.

The second identity is the one that matters. TjT_jTj​ is the cross-domain term: what the other domains’ updates do to domain jjj’s return. Summing keeps it; OPM removes it, whatever its sign. When Tj<0T_j<0Tj​<0 it is interference, and removing it is the point. When Tj>0T_j>0Tj​>0 it is positive transfer, and OPM removes that too. What the term depends on is the surprise: domains couple through overlapping Fishers, not through aligned gradients. In the released 4B specialists merged later in this post, parameter cosines are at most 0.022, yet the math specialist’s update moves the code specialist’s policy by 1.78 times the code specialist’s own drift.

What decoupling buys. Where rounds are lossless, each domain behaves as if it were trained alone: to first order per round in general, and exactly for log-linear policies with linearly independent feature spans, after any number of rounds and for any trainer optimizer whose update depends only on its own history, Adam with persistent state included (Appendix B.2). That gives guarantees multi-task RL does not have.

Proposition 2 · per-domain guarantees, given lossless rounds
  1. Monotone per domain. JjJ_jJj​ decreases only if domain jjj’s solo run does.
  2. Invariant to shares. Domain jjj’s trajectory is independent of the other domains’ batch shares, gradient scales and speeds.
  3. Idle protection. If trainer jjj makes no progress, the anchor moves inside null⁡(Fj)\operatorname{null}(F_j)null(Fj​).
  4. The trigger is the trust region. For any optimizer, Di≤δi+ωD_i\le\delta_i+\omegaDi​≤δi​+ω, with ω\omegaω the KL of one step, and the exact merge’s KL residuals εi\varepsilon_iεi​ satisfy ∑iεi≤∑iDi≤∑i(δi+ω)\sum_i\varepsilon_i\le\sum_iD_i\le\sum_i(\delta_i+\omega)∑i​εi​≤∑i​Di​≤∑i​(δi​+ω).

Item 4 needs no lossless point. Multi-task RL has none of these guarantees. One step of it changes the return of domain jjj by

ΔJj≈η(cj ∇Jj⊤P ∇Jj+∑i≠jci ∇Jj⊤P ∇Ji),\Delta J_j\approx\eta\Big(c_j\,\nabla J_j^\top P\,\nabla J_j+\sum_{i\ne j}c_i\,\nabla J_j^\top P\,\nabla J_i\Big),ΔJj​≈η(cj​∇Jj⊤​P∇Jj​+i=j∑​ci​∇Jj⊤​P∇Ji​),

with cic_ici​ the batch shares and PPP the optimizer’s preconditioner, so under conflict any domain with a small enough share or gradient regresses. Two parameters are enough to see it: with domain 2’s share at 0.2, multi-task SGD drives its return from 0.50 to 0.24, and Adam in a rotated parameterisation drives it to 3×10−43\times10^{-4}3×10−4, while under OPM domain 2 follows the same trajectory for every share and reward scale of domain 1 (Appendix B.5, which also covers forgetting under Cascade RL).

In terms of gradients. The formula above is only the first of three ways multi-task RL couples domains. A shared update adds their gradients, so their directions interfere. A global gradient-norm clip scales every domain’s step by the norm of the sum, so a domain with long, high-norm rollouts shrinks everyone’s step whenever it triggers the clip. And Adam’s second moment is a running average of the squared mixed gradient: wherever one domain’s gradients are large, every domain’s effective learning rate in those coordinates drops, even when the gradients are orthogonal, because in a dense model all domains share all coordinates. OPM cuts all three inside a round. Each trainer has its own optimizer state, clip, learning rate and schedule, which we call optimizer isolation; it is the mechanism behind item 2 of Proposition 2 and behind the Adam example above.

At the merge, the weight a domain gets in a direction is its curvature there, not its gradient norm. A fast domain cannot pull the anchor its way by pushing hard, and a converged domain whose gradients are small but whose curvature is large is protected. Direction is judged in the metric that matters: Euclidean cosines between updates are close to zero at LLM scale, at most 0.022 between the 4B specialists, and say little, while the Fisher overlap that actually couples domains is what (2) weighs. The same choice has a blind spot. A drift that leaves domain jjj’s return unchanged to first order, because it is orthogonal to ∇Jj\nabla J_j∇Jj​, still costs KL, so OPM resists it as firmly as a harmful one. The merge preserves behaviour, not reward, and it pays for that wherever such drift would have been harmless.

Item 4 of Proposition 2 deserves a word: the trigger is the trust region. OPM therefore needs no reference-KL penalty, which matches frontier practice; no arm of our experiments uses one. Because the cubic remainder accumulates per token, the ceiling δi\delta_iδi​ is best set in proportion to domain iii’s response length (Appendix B.6).

What decoupling costs. Removing the cross-domain term removes positive transfer with it, and the price can be stated exactly.

Proposition 3 · the price

Let nnn domains share a direction with common curvature and agreeing objectives, and let each round solve a fraction xxx of it. Along that direction OPM moves xxx, the sum moves nxnxnx, and multi-task RL’s convergence exponent is about nnn times OPM’s. With an interior optimum the sum is better per round iff x<2/(n+1)x<2/(n+1)x<2/(n+1) and diverges iff x>2/nx>2/nx>2/n; with a boundary optimum it is at least as good at every xxx.

A boundary optimum is the common case: pushing up an action that every domain rewards. So OPM has no general rate advantage over a well-tuned multi-task run, and we do not claim one. In KL geometry positive transfer is extra reward-aligned drift, in effect a larger step, and a larger trainer learning rate recovers part of it; merging more often does not, because in lossless directions OPM equals solo training at every interval. With nonlinear policies OPM also carries an error floor of order ηK\eta KηK, set by how far the lossless point lies in parameter space (Appendix B.4). What OPM offers instead of speed are the guarantees above, and when domains conflict, those are worth more than speed.

A controlled toy shows both sides (Appendix E). Four chain tasks share a 704-parameter policy trained with exact gradients over ten seeds, in five variants from strong positive transfer to conflict, with learning rates tuned for both methods. Under positive transfer multi-task RL leads, by 0.20–0.23 in success at 10 steps per task and 0.03–0.05 at 50. Under conflict OPM leads at every budget, 0.97 against at most 0.80 at 50 steps. Across all variants no CG-merged OPM run ended with a task below its starting point, while multi-task RL, task arithmetic and the sum left 20–37% of tasks below it.

Relation to MOPD. Multi-teacher on-policy distillation minimises the reverse KLs to the same trainers on the student’s own rollouts, so the two can be compared directly.

Proposition 4 · MOPD

Let Li(θ)=KL(Pθi∥Pθii)L_i(\theta)=\mathrm{KL}(P^i_\theta\|P^i_{\theta_i})Li​(θ)=KL(Pθi​∥Pθi​i​) be MOPD’s loss for teacher iii. Then Ji(θ)≤Ji(θi)+Li(θ)/2J_i(\theta)\le J_i(\theta_i)+\sqrt{L_i(\theta)/2}Ji​(θ)≤Ji​(θi​)+Li​(θ)/2​. The OPM point is a stationary point of ∑iLi\sum_iL_i∑i​Li​ to second order, with gradient O(∥⋅∥2)O(\|\cdot\|^2)O(∥⋅∥2) against O(∥⋅∥)O(\|\cdot\|)O(∥⋅∥) for task arithmetic and the sum, and in a lossless round it is the global minimiser to third order.

The bound is Pinsker’s inequality: at its optimum the MOPD student equals its teachers, and it can exceed them only by not converging or through an added outcome reward. Liu et al. showed that MOPD is Fisher merging to second order; Proposition 4 adds the lossless statement and which Fisher to use. OPM reaches the same point without student rollouts, and it has no fixed teacher: each round’s θi\theta_iθi​ is retrained on reward from the last merge. A rendezvous needs no environment interaction, while a round of MOPD needs fresh rollouts in every domain, which for agentic domains means sandboxes running for minutes per episode.

The scope of these guarantees. Theorem 1 and Proposition 2 hold exactly only in lossless rounds, where some merged point keeps every trainer’s policy. We have not shown that such rounds exist at LLM scale, and the one-shot 4B merge below suggests they do not quite: even after 30 CG iterations, the merged model’s KL to the specialists is still 16% of how far they drifted. In practice the guarantees hold approximately, as closely as that residual is small, which is why the main runs log it at every rendezvous. Appendix B gives the status and proof of every statement, and lists what is not claimed.

#Making the merge cheap

A merge is only worth having if it is cheap next to the training it interrupts. This section works out what a merge costs, measures it at 9B, and asks what changes at frontier scale, where models have hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, layers are mixtures of experts, and rollouts arrive asynchronously from inference engines that do not match the trainer exactly.

What a merge costs. Formula (2) cannot be formed for a model of this size, since the Fisher has as many rows as the model has parameters. It can be solved, though: conjugate gradient (CG) only ever needs products FivF_ivFi​v . Each trainer computes its own product on its own GPUs, at its own weights, over the rollouts it has cached, and one all-reduce per iteration adds the products up. A rendezvous with KKK CG iterations and LLL line-search candidates, on NFN_FNF​ Fisher tokens per trainer, spread over the SSS training steps of NstepN_{\rm step}Nstep​ tokens between rendezvous, adds

overhead  ≈  (K cFVP+L cfwd) NFS Nstep\text{overhead}\;\approx\;\frac{(K\,c_{\rm FVP}+L\,c_{\rm fwd})\,N_F}{S\,N_{\rm step}}overhead≈SNstep​(KcFVP​+Lcfwd​)NF​​

to training compute, where cFVPc_{\rm FVP}cFVP​ and cfwdc_{\rm fwd}cfwd​ are the costs of a product and of a forward pass per token, in units of one training token. Two consequences follow, and they pull in different directions. The compute ratio does not depend on model size. A Fisher-vector product touches the same parameters per token as a training step does, so both scale with the active parameters, and a trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model pays the same fraction as a dense model of its active size. Memory and communication do depend on it, because they scale with all the parameters. CG keeps fp32 vectors as long as the model, and four of them take as much memory as the training state itself. Each iteration also all-reduces one of them across trainers: 4 TB at a trillion parameters, a matter of seconds inside one cluster and impractical between clusters.

What we measured at 9B. On MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B the product dominates everything else. We compute it exactly, with the true per-token Fisher rather than the empirical one, in fp32 and with finite differences in logit space. It costs 6.9 GPU-milliseconds per token, so cFVP≈16c_{\rm FVP}\approx16cFVP​≈16 bf16 gradient passes; about half of that is the backward pass and 40% the finite-difference forward passes. Communication and the n×nn\times nn×n algebra were negligible on one node, and keeping the CG vectors in CPU memory, a tempting way to save GPU memory, made every product three times slower. The guarded merge below uses four products and four forward passes and takes about ten minutes. Everything that follows is about shrinking cFVPNFc_{\rm FVP}N_FcFVP​NF​.

Conjugate gradient overshoots. Our first attempt failed in an instructive way. Plain CG, started from the summed update, made the held-out residual worse at each of its first iterations, even though the quadratic model was accurate along the directions it took (κ\kappaκ between 0.87 and 1.0). The trouble is where CG looks first. Its earliest directions are the Fisher’s stiffest, about 10710^7107 times stiffer than typical ones, and along them the KL saturates within 0.3% of the update norm. A finite-difference product measures a secant across its step, and across a saturating stretch the secant is flatter than the curvature at the start: it underestimated the curvature sixteen-fold at a logit step of 0.3 and by 40% at 0.03. Seeing too little curvature, CG stepped too far.

The fix is a guarded merge. Use a finite-difference logit step of 0.01, run three CG iterations from the summed update dΣd_\SigmadΣ​, and choose γ∈{0,14,12,1}\gamma\in\{0,\tfrac14,\tfrac12,1\}γ∈{0,41​,21​,1} along d(γ)=dΣ+γ(xCG−dΣ)d(\gamma)=d_\Sigma+\gamma(x_{\rm CG}-d_\Sigma)d(γ)=dΣ​+γ(xCG​−dΣ​) by the true KL on held-out rollouts of the trainers. Since γ=0\gamma=0γ=0 is the sum, the chosen point is never worse than the sum up to estimation error, and no quadratic assumption is needed for that (Proposition 5, Appendix C).

Three iterations plus the line search cut the residual by 36% relative to the sum (13.35 to 8.57 nats) and by 72% relative to averaging, in about ten minutes: four Fisher-vector products and four forward passes. The full CG step never beats the half step, five or more iterations make things worse, and a large finite-difference step of 0.3 blows the full step’s residual up to 113 nats after two iterations and 215 after three. This guarded merge is the default in all our training runs. It is one test case, two domains on one model, and the main runs log the residual for every γ\gammaγ at every rendezvous.

Levers at frontier scale. We now reason about models at frontier size, hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, and lay out the optimisations and analysis we expect OPM to need there. Four levers act on the cost of a merge; three more choices fit it into asynchronous training. The runs that would confirm each are listed at the end of the section.

Fewer tokens. Most of the Fisher sits on a small fraction of tokens. For one token, the Fisher in logit space is diag(p)−pp⊤\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^\topdiag(p)−pp⊤, the covariance of the next-token distribution, and its size is its trace, 1−∑apa21-\sum_ap_a^21−∑a​pa2​. On a token the model is sure about, ppp is nearly one-hot and the trace is nearly zero, so the token adds almost nothing to FivF_ivFi​v however much it cost to process. Reasoning traces are mostly such tokens: only about a fifth are high-entropy forks, and those carry most of the RL signal . We can therefore sample tokens with probability proportional to 1−∑apa21-\sum_ap_a^21−∑a​pa2​, weight each by the inverse of that probability so the estimate stays unbiased, and keep only the top few logits of each token to trim the vocabulary head. If the Fisher is as concentrated as the gradient, this cuts cFVPNFc_{\rm FVP}N_FcFVP​NF​ several-fold at little cost in accuracy.

Exact, cheaper products. The finite difference is both a cost and the cause of the overshoot above. A Jacobian-vector product followed by a vector-Jacobian product computes the Gauss–Newton product exactly, with no step to tune. The curvature CG sees is then the true local curvature, and the guard becomes a safety net rather than a requirement. Running the products in bf16 with fp32 accumulation cuts cFVPc_{\rm FVP}cFVP​ further, as long as the merge’s own arithmetic stays in fp32, above the bf16 floor. The risk is engineering: forward-mode differentiation has to pass through fused attention and expert kernels, which few training stacks support today.

A subspace solve. CG searches the whole parameter space, but the trainers’ updates already span most of what a merge needs. Restricting the merge to θˉ+∑kckΔk\bar\theta+\sum_kc_k\Delta_kθˉ+∑k​ck​Δk​ turns (2) into an n×nn\times nn×n linear system whose entries, ∑iΔj⊤FiΔk\sum_i\Delta_j^\top F_i\Delta_k∑i​Δj⊤​Fi​Δk​, are the curvature the domains assign to each pair of updates. The result is task arithmetic with Fisher-optimal coefficients, and splitting the inner products by layer or by expert gives one coefficient per block from the same products. Each trainer computes FiΔkF_i\Delta_kFi​Δk​ for every kkk on its own data, in parallel, and sends n2n^2n2 numbers. That is nnn products instead of KKK sequential ones, so it does not always save compute, but it removes every full-size all-reduce beyond the exchange of updates that any merge needs, which is what makes trainers in different clusters feasible. The subspace solution is also a better starting point for CG than the sum, and a rendezvous can warm-start from the previous one.

Experts and memory. Mixture-of-experts layers give the Fisher a block structure. An expert’s block sums only over the tokens routed to it, so where domains use different experts their blocks barely overlap and (2) reduces to the plain sum there; the coupling, and the CG work, concentrate in attention, embeddings, shared experts and the router. Routing also adds a locality condition of its own. A merge that flips the top-kkk choice for many tokens moves them onto different experts, outside any quadratic model, so the fraction of flipped routes belongs next to κ\kappaκ among the diagnostics logged at every rendezvous. The larger frontier cost is memory: nnn trainers hold nnn training states of about 16 bytes per parameter, 16 TB each at a trillion parameters. Grouping domains (Discussion) divides that by the group size. Low-rank trainers would divide it further: each domain trains an adapter on the shared anchor, and each rendezvous merges the adapters’ updates in their span and folds the result into the anchor. LoRA matches full fine-tuning in RL even at very low rank ; whether the merge keeps its guarantees under that restriction is open.

Asynchronous RL and training–inference mismatch. Frontier rollouts are not quite on-policy. Inference engines run weights a few steps old, with different kernels and often lower precision, so the token probabilities they sample from differ from the trainer’s, and trainers correct the gap with truncated importance sampling ,. This touches the core of OPM: the range property holds because the gradient and the Fisher are expectations under the same distribution. Three choices keep it intact.

A logit-space Fisher. Compute the Fisher per token as Jt⊤(diag(pt)−ptpt⊤)JtJ_t^\top\big(\mathrm{diag}(p_t)-p_tp_t^\top\big)J_tJt⊤​(diag(pt​)−pt​pt⊤​)Jt​, with ptp_tpt​ the trainer’s own recomputed next-token distribution, rather than from the score of the sampled token. The sampled token is exactly where staleness and mismatch enter, and this form never uses it: it averages over the whole vocabulary under the trainer’s distribution. It is also centred by construction, because diag(p)−pp⊤\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^\topdiag(p)−pp⊤ is the covariance of the one-hot token under ppp. A Fisher built from sampled scores would need per-token importance weights and explicit score centring, since the score has mean zero only under the trainer’s own policy. What remains is a shift in which histories get visited, of the size of the per-token KL between the rollout and trainer policies, which truncated prefix weights absorb.

A rendezvous is one more policy lag. After a merge, the rollouts still in flight were sampled by the pre-merge weights, so they are stale by the merge’s displacement. The importance weights the trainer already applies handle that, as long as the per-token KL a merge introduces stays within the range those weights are tuned for. This gives a concrete reason to bound a merge per token rather than per rollout.

Hidden latency. The merge need not stop training. Solve it on a snapshot of the trainers while they keep stepping, then add θ+−θsnapshot\theta^{+}-\theta_{\rm snapshot}θ+−θsnapshot​ to every trainer. The correction is a few steps stale, which asynchronous RL already tolerates by design.

All of this sits on a floor set by the serving stack. Casting an fp32 specialist to bf16 moves its policy by 25–40% of its RL drift (Side findings), so triggers, residual targets and the guard all have to sit above the mismatch between the engines that sample and the trainer that learns.

#A first test on released specialists

Before training anything, we can test the merge rule on RL specialists that someone else trained. Wu et al. released five 300-step GRPO specialists of Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 in fp32 (math, science, code, instruction following and a tool-using agent), together with their own task-arithmetic, mixed-RL and MOPD models and their evaluation. We merged the five specialists once with (2): ten CG iterations from the summed update, with exact per-token Fisher-vector products on 256 of each specialist’s own rollouts, and no training or student rollouts. This tests the operator, not the loop, and in its least favourable setting: a single merge after 75 to 248 nats of drift. It also lets us check three things the theory predicts.

The merge does what the theory says. The quadratic model still holds at this drift: the locality ratio κ\kappaκ toward the merged points is 0.96–1.17, where an exact quadratic gives 1, and plain CG did not overshoot here. The merge keeps far more of each specialist than the other rules do. On held-out prompts its KL residual is 0.31 of the drift, against 0.52 for task arithmetic, 0.34 for the released MOPD model and 1.12 for the sum, and 0.16 after 30 iterations. Where a domain barely sees the others’ updates, the round is close to lossless: the residual is 0.025 of the drift for the instruction-following specialist and 0.037 for the agent, against 0.26 for task arithmetic.

On benchmarks it beats task arithmetic and MOPD. On the domain-balanced mean of Table 3, the one-shot OPM merge is 1.26 points above task arithmetic and 0.78 above the released MOPD model, with no rollouts beyond the 256 per domain behind the Fisher. Paired intervals for this mean are being recomputed; on the eight-benchmark mean of Wu et al., which counts AIME and LiveCodeBench twice, the same gaps are 1.68 ± 0.42 and 1.11 ± 0.40 over prompts. The clearest single case is IFBench: 50.5, against 40.4 for task arithmetic and 48.9 for the instruction-following specialist itself. Deploying the same merge in fp32 adds about a point more (Side findings).

Where domains help each other, the sum wins. At the same bf16 precision, plain summation beats the OPM merge by 0.58 points, mostly on AIME, although its KL residual is almost four times larger; with 30 CG iterations the gap shrinks to 0.16, within run-to-run noise. This is Theorem 1 at work, not a failure of the metric. Math, science and code help each other: the summed model beats every reasoning specialist on its own benchmark, and the estimated cross-domain term is positive on all three, 0.17 to 0.26 of each domain’s own gain. The OPM merge pulls each specialist back toward its own behaviour and gives that transfer up, exactly as the theory says it should. Instruction following and the agent barely see the others’ updates, and there the sum and the OPM merge tie. The KL residual measures how much of each specialist is kept, not how much reward is gained.

What this shows, and what it does not. One-shot at 4B, the operator earns its keep against task arithmetic and MOPD but not against the sum, and since the quadratic model held, what limits it is overlap between the reasoning domains rather than locality. That already makes a one-shot OPM merge a strong post-hoc tool for released specialists. One caveat cuts the other way: a Fisher computed on the base model’s rollouts instead of each specialist’s own is worse in KL but ties on benchmarks, so the case for the on-policy metric does not rest on this experiment. What merging during training must add is the rest of Why meet often: calibrated weights and a next round of RL that repairs the residual. The main experiment and the frequency sweep test that. Appendix D has the full residual tables, the interference matrix, the other merge variants and the evaluation protocol.

#Main results

Setting. The main comparison trains MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B on eight domains that public frontier recipes train with RL: software engineering, terminal, cyber, knowledge work, search, tool use, hard math and instruction following. Verifiers are executable tests, rule checkers, state checks and, for knowledge work, a rubric judge. Agentic episodes run up to 150 turns and 128k tokens. All arms share one RL framework (slime), one GRPO recipe, one chat template with thinking on, the same verifiers, harnesses and evaluation, and no reference-KL penalty. The budget is matched in environment rollouts per domain, counting MOPD’s student rollouts. GPU-hours and wall-clock are reported separately.Appendix F gives every detail.

  • A4 · OPM. Eight trainers, KL-triggered rendezvous, and the guarded merge described above.

#How often to merge

The rendezvous frequency is the one knob that moves OPM along the frequency axis, from merge-after (a single rendezvous at the end) toward multi-task RL. Why meet often gave four reasons to merge early and one thing frequency cannot fix; this section tests them. Between the two ends sits a cheap compromise, merge-then-polish: the specialists train apart as usual, and a few rendezvous at the end of the run bring them back together. It keeps the training pipeline unchanged and adds the repair that a single merge lacks.

In the toy the interval matters sharply. At 50 steps per task, merging every 1, 5, 10, 25 or 50 steps gave 0.97, 0.96, 0.93, 0.34 and 0.08. A KL trigger beat a fixed interval with a similar number of rendezvous, 0.987 against 0.88. Frequent rendezvous also passed more transfer into an idle task: under the exact merge, +0.48 at an interval of 1 against −0.21 at 50. The theory attributes this to calibration along shared directions, not to transfer through lossless ones, and part of it is unexplained (Appendix E). The merge-frequency experiment below measures the same curve on the 9B model.

#Adding a skill, containing a fault

Because each domain has its own trainer, OPM can change its set of domains mid-run, and a fault in one domain reaches the others only through the merge. Two demonstrations test whether that matters in practice. Both branch from the seed-1 runs and apply the same intervention to multi-task RL.

Demo 1: adding a skill. At half the budget, competitive code, a domain no arm has trained on, is added. OPM starts a code trainer from the current anchor at the next rendezvous; multi-task RL resumes with a re-mixed nine-domain quota. We measure how many rollouts and how much wall-clock code needs to approach its specialist, the largest drop on the eight existing domains, and the extra cost. Idle protection predicts that the existing domains hold wherever the new trainer’s Fisher range is independent of theirs.

#Side findings

Measuring merges at the level of policies, in exact fp32, turned up five findings that matter beyond OPM. Appendix G has the numbers.

Orthogonal is not independent. The released specialists’ task vectors are nearly orthogonal, with cosines of at most 0.022, yet they interfere strongly. The math specialist’s update moves the code specialist’s policy by 1.78 times the code specialist’s own drift. Interference lives in the Fisher, which weights directions by how much the policy cares about them, and the directions RL moves are thousands of times stiffer than random ones. Cosine similarity of task vectors is a poor guide to whether two specialists can be merged.

“Sparse” RL updates are a bf16 artefact. In fp32 the specialists’ updates are dense: 99.996% of entries are nonzero, with a median size of about 2−112^{-11}2−11 relative to the weights. Rounding the specialists to bf16 leaves only 18% of the update entries nonzero, and the rounded update has cosine 0.57 with the true one and an 84% relative error. Claims that RL makes sparse updates should be checked against fp32 weights.

There is a bf16 floor. Casting an fp32 specialist to bf16 moves its policy by 25–40% of its whole RL drift, measured in KL on its own rollouts. The same merged model scores 1.0 points higher (1.30 ± 0.34 on the eight-benchmark mean) deployed in fp32 than in bf16. Any merge, trigger or residual threshold has to sit above this floor, and scoring has to run in true fp32.

KL residual is not reward loss. The sum has the largest KL residual of any merge and the best benchmark mean at bf16. Behind this is an exact decomposition: a return change is the reward-weighted log-likelihood ratio plus a term bounded by the KL. To first order it is ρ σ2ε\rho\,\sigma\sqrt{2\varepsilon}ρσ2ε​, with ρ\rhoρ the correlation between reward and the log-ratio, σ\sigmaσ the reward’s standard deviation and ε\varepsilonε the KL residual. A large residual costs little reward when ρ≈0\rho\approx0ρ≈0 and helps when ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0. Pinsker-type bounds are vacuous above about 2 nats, while specialists drift 75–248 nats.

When the sum beats OPM. The sum wins exactly when domains help each other, and that can be measured per domain: how much of the others’ updates domain jjj’s Fisher sees (its visibility), and the sign of the transfer term TjT_jTj​. The 4B reasoning domains are in this regime. The instruction-following and agent domains barely see the others’ updates, so the sum and the OPM merge tie there. The toy’s conflict variants are the opposite regime, where OPM wins. Logging TjT_jTj​ at each rendezvous tells a practitioner which regime a run is in.

#Discussion

When to use it. OPM is a decoupling device. It pays where coupling hurts: domains that conflict, many domains with small shares each, rollout latencies that differ by orders of magnitude, domains whose gradient scales differ enough to fight over a shared clip or Adam state, and teams that want to add, drop, tune or fix a domain without retraining the rest. It gives ground where coupling helps: when domains share skills, multi-task RL or the plain sum moves faster along the shared directions, and OPM recovers that only through larger trainer steps. The transfer term and visibility, both logged at every rendezvous, tell which situation a run is in.

Trade-offs. Every rendezvous costs a merge, about ten minutes on a 9B model with the guarded solver, and a synchronisation, since every trainer waits for the merged model. Meeting often buys locality, calibrated weights and repair, and pays for them in merges; merge-then-polish pays for only a few. Memory grows with the number of trainers, one model copy per domain, which grouping domains reduces. And decoupling gives up transfer along shared directions, which a larger trainer learning rate recovers only in part.

Limitations. The guarantees assume lossless rounds, and we have not shown that they exist at LLM scale. In the 4B merge the residual after 30 CG iterations is still 16% of drift on held-out prompts, and the reasoning domains overlap. The informative statements at realistic drift are second-order or about KL, not reward. The trajectory Fisher grows with tokens, so long-response domains get more weight in shared directions. OPM keeps one model copy per domain in memory. The Fisher is estimated from a subsample, and the evidence for the guarded merge comes from one two-domain test. In the one-shot merge, a stale metric tied the on-policy one on benchmarks. All results are at 4B and 9B on dense models; mixture-of-experts models and larger scales are untested.

Related work. The barycenter objective comes from Distral and Divide-and-Conquer RL ,, and policy distillation into one network from Rusu et al.. The merge operator comes from Fisher merging, RegMean and MaTS ,,, all applied once and in supervised settings. Liu et al. showed that MOPD is Fisher merging to second order. WARP iterates merging and re-initialisation across parallel RLHF runs on one task . Co-Evolving Policy Distillation couples per-domain GRPO branches during training through distillation , and M2A merges a math vector into an agent only along the null space of agent-critical activations , a close cousin of Theorem 1. Federated learning studies periodic averaging under heterogeneity ,,,, including function-space aggregation , federated GRPO and federated natural policy gradient for multi-task RL . As far as we know, OPM is the first to use the on-policy trajectory Fisher inside RL, where Theorem 1 holds, and the first to trigger a weight merge on trajectory KL. Appendix H discusses each in detail.

An extension: grouped OPM. Frontier runs train dozens of domains, and the published evidence on how they interact is mixed in a way that looks like structure rather than noise. Reasoning domains tend to help each other: RLVR across domains shows small mutual interference and synergy among reasoning-intensive domains , and math, code and science benefit from cross-domain training while logic, simulation and tabular reasoning need in-domain data . Other pairs conflict. Math-only GRPO on Qwen2.5-7B lowers its code average from 67.46 to 29.59 ; the instruction-following specialist of Wu et al. lowers BFCL from 63.9 to 54.1; models trained on mixed-domain batches consistently underperform the best domain experts ; and in a Code → Math → QA → writing curriculum, math falls from 66.49 to 57.66 during the later stages while the full-model gradient cosine between math and QA stays close to zero . That last case is interference a gradient cosine cannot see and a Fisher can.

This suggests a middle ground between one trainer for all domains and one per domain. Group the domains that help each other into a single multi-task trainer, so their transfer is kept inside the group, and give groups that conflict separate trainers that meet through the OPM merge. One group is multi-task RL; one domain per group is OPM. Theorem 1 then holds between groups: each group is protected from the others, and nothing is protected inside a group. The quantities that decide the grouping are the ones OPM already logs at every rendezvous, the visibility of one domain’s update in another’s Fisher and the sign of the transfer term TjT_jTj​. Domains with positive TjT_jTj​ and high mutual visibility belong together; a pair with negative TjT_jTj​ and high visibility is the one to split. Since a rendezvous is cheap, the grouping can change during a run, for example by splitting a group when its members’ transfer terms turn negative. Grouping also cuts OPM’s memory cost from one model copy per domain to one per group. We have not run it yet; it is the natural next experiment once the main runs show where the 9B domains fall.

Conclusion. Combining RL domains is a choice of how often and in which geometry. Choosing often and in the on-policy KL geometry gives a merge with a closed form that removes cross-domain terms of both signs. It guarantees per-domain progress where domains can be separated, costs speed where they agree, and takes about ten minutes on a 9B model once the solver is guarded. Merged once at 4B, it beats task arithmetic and MOPD and loses to the plain sum, for reasons the theory predicts. Whether merging often closes that gap, and what OPM buys against multi-task RL and MOPD at scale, are what the pending results above will settle.

A protected cascade keeps idle trainers in the merge with Δj=0\Delta_j=0Δj​=0; in a lossless round the anchor moves inside null⁡Fj\operatorname{null}F_jnullFj​, exactly for log-linear policies. B.6 The trigger, locality and the choice of δ

The trigger is a trust region [T] for (a) and (c), [P] second order for (b). Let rounds end when Di≥δiD_i\ge\delta_iDi​≥δi​ for some iii (here a common δ\deltaδ), with one-step overshoot ω\omegaω. Then Di≤δ+ωD_i\le\delta+\omegaDi​≤δ+ω for every trainer, whatever its optimizer. (a) The exact minimiser of (1) has ∑iεi≤∑iDi≤n(δ+ω)\sum_i\varepsilon_i\le\sum_iD_i\le n(\delta+\omega)∑i​εi​≤∑i​Di​≤n(δ+ω), because the old anchor is feasible. An inexact merge inherits this only if its candidate set contains a point with residual at most ∑iDi\sum_iD_i∑i​Di​; the production merge guarantees only “no worse than the sum” (Proposition 5). (b) On domain jjj the new anchor is within ∥d∥Fj≤2εj(2)+2Dj(2)\|d\|_{F_j}\le\sqrt{2\varepsilon^{(2)}_j}+\sqrt{2D^{(2)}_j}∥d∥Fj​​≤2εj(2)​​+2Dj(2)​​ of the old one. (c) Jj(θˉ+)≥Jj(θˉ)+Gj−εj/2J_j(\bar\theta^{+})\ge J_j(\bar\theta)+G_j-\sqrt{\varepsilon_j/2}Jj​(θˉ+)≥Jj​(θˉ)+Gj​−εj​/2​, with Gj=Jj(θj)−Jj(θˉ)G_j=J_j(\theta_j)-J_j(\bar\theta)Gj​=Jj​(θj​)−Jj​(θˉ). Without a reference KL, the trainers’ local solution is not a natural-gradient step, and nothing makes drift level off: the trigger is the only thing that caps drift. KL penalties toward a shared model appear in federated policy gradient ; OPM replaces the penalty by the trigger and moves the anchor at every rendezvous.

Locality [P], lossless rounds, per-round displacements of order h=ℓ/Rh=\ell/Rh=ℓ/R, with ℓ\ellℓ the Fisher path length. The residual of a round is O(h3)O(h^3)O(h3), and O(h4)O(h^4)O(h4) along null directions, so over RRR rounds it totals O(ℓ3/R2)O(\ell^3/R^2)O(ℓ3/R2). One-shot merging is R=1R=1R=1. Under real conflict each round leaves a second-order residual whose first-order reward cost does not shrink with merge frequency.

Endpoint-Fisher collapse [T] for the logistic case, [C] for many rounds. One trainer pushes a logit to z1z_1z1​; an idle trainer stays at 0. Formula (2) returns z+=f(z1)z1/(f(z1)+14)→0z^{+}=f(z_1)z_1/(f(z_1)+\tfrac14)\to0z+=f(z1​)z1​/(f(z1​)+41​)→0, with f=σ(1−σ)f=\sigma(1-\sigma)f=σ(1−σ), while the exact barycenter keeps σ(z+)=(σ(z1)+12)/2→34\sigma(z^{+})=(\sigma(z_1)+\tfrac12)/2\to\tfrac34σ(z+)=(σ(z1​)+21​)/2→43​. The locality ratio κ=KL(1)/(16 KL(14))\kappa=\mathrm{KL}(1)/(16\,\mathrm{KL}(\tfrac14))κ=KL(1)/(16KL(41​)) is 1.00, 1.35, 1.92 and 8.9 after 1, 10, 20 and 200 steps, so the test κ>1.5\kappa>1.5κ>1.5 flags the collapse within 20 steps. In a multi-round tabular check at fixed budget, as the interval grows from 1 to 120, the quadratic merge’s idle-domain gain falls from 0.43 to 0.11 and the exact barycenter’s from 0.43 to 0.29.

Repair and data validity [T]. After a rendezvous trainers resume on-policy RL, so a round’s residual costs steps rather than final quality: the final bound involves only the last round. Whole-trajectory importance weights have χ2≥eKL−1\chi^2\ge e^{\mathrm{KL}}-1χ2≥eKL−1, so at residuals of tens of nats no trajectory-level reuse is possible, for OPM or anyone else. What makes in-flight reuse possible is per-token importance sampling, as in truncated importance sampling and IcePop , where χtok2≈2εtok\chi^2_{\rm tok}\approx2\varepsilon_{\rm tok}χtok2​≈2εtok​. One-shot per-token residuals at 4B are 0.01–0.44 nats (sum: 0.03–0.07).

Choosing δ [P], partly [C]. (i) Locality is a per-token condition, so set δi=ℓˉiτtok\delta_i=\bar\ell_i\tau_{\rm tok}δi​=ℓˉi​τtok​, with ℓˉi\bar\ell_iℓˉi​ the mean response length, or trigger on per-token KL. At 4B, κ≈1\kappa\approx1κ≈1 toward the merged points at 0.02–0.04 nats per token. (ii) The Fisher sample needs many more tokens than the effective rank of the subspace in which domains see each other, so it grows with the drift budget. (iii) Rounds per unit of Fisher path scale as δ−1/2\delta^{-1/2}δ−1/2; take the largest δ\deltaδ meeting (i) and (ii) within the merge-cost budget. (iv) Record κ\kappaκ and the in-sample against held-out KL gap at each rendezvous to tell estimation failures from locality failures.

An OPM rendezvous needs none: a few Fisher-vector products per trainer on cached rollouts plus forward passes for the line search.

B.9 What is not claimed

  • No general rate advantage over well-tuned multi-task RL. OPM is slower along agreeing shared directions, up to nnn times in the exponent, and has an O(ηK)O(\eta K)O(ηK) floor with nonlinear networks.
  • No positive transfer within a round. Frequency does not change this for exact lossless merges (refuted: “frequent rendezvous captures transfer”).
  • No reward guarantee at realistic trajectory KL. Pinsker-type bounds are vacuous above about 2 nats; 4B specialists drift 75–248 nats.
  • Lossless points are assumed, not shown, at LLM scale. At 4B the residual after 30 CG iterations is still 15% of drift.
  • Speed invariance holds only in lossless directions or with round-solving trainers; under conflict, step sizes act as weights.
  • No invariance to rollout length: long-response domains weigh more in shared directions.
  • Exact gradients and Fishers are assumed except in Proposition 5 and the CG step criterion; the tabular rate is inherited from the discounted literature.

Moving the vectors to the GPU took one product on 11k tokens from 66 s to 19 s. One product over about 36k tokens takes 100–120 s. Further levers we have not yet adopted: running the vector-Jacobian product in bf16 (it is linear in the cotangent, and bf16 forward+backward costs 0.44 against 3.6 in fp32), TF32 finite-difference forwards with fp32 refinement, subsampling the curvature batch as Hessian-free optimisation and TRPO do ,, warm starts across rendezvous, and running the solve on spare GPUs while training continues.

The 9B test case. Two trainers branched from MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B: math for 40 steps and instruction following for 30. Fisher-vector products on 32 rollouts per trainer, residuals on held-out rollouts, damping μ=10−3\mu=10^{-3}μ=10−3 of the mean curvature. Held-out drifts 76.4 and 49.0 nats. Along the sum-minus-own direction the quadratic model holds, κ\kappaκ 0.87–1.0. With a finite-difference step of 0.3, CG with the full step gave 112.7 nats after two iterations and 214.7 after three; with step 0.01 the numbers are those of Table 2. The per-trainer residuals at the chosen point (three iterations, γ=12\gamma=\tfrac12γ=21​) are 3.0 and 5.5 nats, against 5.2 and 8.1 for the sum.

System. Each trainer is an ordinary GRPO trainer with a hook: after each optimizer step it runs the frozen anchor on about one rollout in eight to update its drift. At a rendezvous, the merge runs as a collective across trainers: every trainer computes its own Fisher-vector products on its own GPUs and cached tokens (a forward-mode pass for the change in logits, multiplication by diag⁡(π)−ππ⊤\operatorname{diag}(\pi)-\pi\pi^\topdiag(π)−ππ⊤, and a backward pass), one all-reduce per iteration sums them, and the line search scores the candidates on held-out rollouts. Rendezvous are non-blocking: a slow trainer contributes its current weights and its latest batch’s Fisher. Each trainer keeps its optimizer moments, learning rate, batch size, rollout servers and sandboxes; the trainers share only a weight format. Logged at every rendezvous: drift, residual per γ\gammaγ, the chosen γ\gammaγ, CG iterations, tokens, wall-clock, κ\kappaκ, and TjT_jTj​.

Artefacts. Base Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and the five fp32 specialists of Wu et al., with their training and test data and their verl-based code. Their recipe: GRPO with 128 prompts × 16 rollouts per step, learning rate 10−610^{-6}10−6, 300 steps, responses up to 16,384 tokens, temperature 1, and a KL loss to the base with coefficient 0.001, which is effectively no penalty. The released task-arithmetic merge uses λ=0.6\lambda=0.6λ=0.6 over the fp32 specialists and is stored in bf16. Casting each fp32 specialist to bf16 reproduces the released bf16 checkpoint bit for bit.

Evaluation. The protocol of Wu et al.: mean over 32 samples, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, responses up to 16,384 tokens, non-thinking mode, their scorers for each benchmark, and a local sandbox for LiveCodeBench. Our base, MOPD and IF-specialist IFBench scores (30.7 / 46.7 / 48.9) reproduce the published 30.3 / 47.3 / 49.0. Table 3 reports AIME 2025 and 2026 pooled, LiveCodeBench v6 only and a domain-balanced mean; the paired differences quoted with ± in this appendix are on the eight-benchmark mean of Wu et al., which weights AIME and LiveCodeBench twice. Our task-arithmetic point is bit-identical to the released merge after the bf16 cast; evaluating both gives −0.32 ± 0.22, the run-to-run noise floor. The sum writes the longest code answers (about 6,000 tokens against 3,600 for task arithmetic; 5–7% hit the cap), the OPM points about 4,400–4,900.

E. The toy, with the corrected baseline

Setting. A 704-parameter policy shared by four chain tasks with horizons 2, 6, 16 and 16, trained with exact policy gradients and Adam; returns, gradients, Fishers and KLs are computed in closed form. Ten random problems per cell. Five variants set the cross-task effect: the original (gradient cosine −0.16; training one task changes another by −0.16), pos-soft (+0.21; +0.10), pos-strong (+0.50; +0.19), neg (−0.24; −0.19) and mixed (−0.19; −0.13). OPM uses an interval of 5 steps and 10 CG iterations unless noted. The code will be released with the main runs.

Correction. The previous version of this post compared OPM with multi-task RL at its default learning rate, 0.688 against 0.963 on the original variant. Tuning the multi-task learning rate over 1–16× its default raises it to 0.949. The comparison below tunes both.

At smaller budgets the positive variants favour multi-task RL more strongly. Against multi-task RL at 4× its rate, OPM (CG-10, default rate) trails by 0.23 / 0.20 at 10 steps per task, 0.18 / 0.10 at 25 and 0.05 / 0.03 at 50 (pos-soft / pos-strong). Under conflict, OPM leads at every budget once both rates are tuned (at 25 steps, 0.980 / 0.986 for OPM at 4× against 0.762 / 0.776 for the best multi-task rate, neg / mixed).

Transfer into an idle task (the task’s trainer is in the merge but does not train), 10 steps: periodic sum −0.13 / +0.13 / +0.33 / −0.19 / −0.15 over the five variants; exact OPM −0.07 / −0.08 / −0.11 / −0.03 / −0.05; OPM CG-10 −0.01 / +0.04 / +0.19 / −0.03 / −0.01. OPM blocks positive transfer into idle tasks, as Theorem 1 predicts. A task absent from the run receives about as much transfer under OPM as under multi-task RL or the sum (pos-strong: +0.30, +0.24, +0.33). In a sweep of the interval at 50 steps (pos-strong), idle-task transfer under exact OPM is +0.48 at an interval of 1, more than the sum’s +0.38, and −0.21 at 50; CG-10 goes from +0.49 to +0.13. A tabular check of the same quantity gives 0.43 for OPM against 0.45 for the sum, so we suspect the excess at interval 1 comes from summing Adam steps, but it is unconfirmed.

A reward-aware merge. Adding the trainers’ gradients to the merge, θˉ+A+∑i(FiΔi+gi/βm)\bar\theta+A^{+}\sum_i(F_i\Delta_i+g_i/\beta_m)θˉ+A+∑i​(Fi​Δi​+gi​/βm​), looks like a way to recover transfer. Because gi∈range⁡Fig_i\in\operatorname{range}F_igi​∈rangeFi​, it is exactly OPM applied to trainers that each took one extra natural-gradient step (numerical identity error at most 2.6×10−32.6\times10^{-3}2.6×10−3). Its gain is flat across variants (+0.21 to +0.26 at 10 steps), a step-size effect that OPM with a 4× trainer rate reproduces within about 0.02. It remains an ablation.

Guarantees. Pinsker’s bound held in all 79,012 trainer–round pairs. OPM CG-10 never lost more than a trainer’s gain in a round, and no CG-merged run ended with a task below its starting point; multi-task RL, task arithmetic and the sum left 20–37% of tasks below it in the conflict variants.

Results from the first toy version (same problem, original variant, 50 steps per task). These do not depend on the multi-task learning rate, except the last item, which uses multi-task RL at its default rate.

  • Metric: Fisher from the trainer’s current rollouts 0.96; from the anchor’s, one round old, 0.95; from the base model’s, never refreshed, 0.13.
  • Operator: average 0.48, diagonal Fisher 0.47, layer Grams 0.62, K-FAC 0.71, sum 0.75, ten likelihood steps 0.84, CG with 3 iterations 0.82, with 10 iterations 0.955, exact 0.963. Cheap layer-wise approximations did worse than the plain sum.
  • Interval: every 1, 5, 10, 25, 50 steps gave 0.97, 0.96, 0.93, 0.34, 0.08. With 100 steps per task, a KL trigger of 0.3 nats reached 0.987 with 6.6 rendezvous; a fixed interval with 5 rendezvous reached 0.88.
  • Staleness after a rendezvous at interval 5: median residual 0.0003 nats and effective sample size 99.9% for OPM, against 0.059 nats and 86% for the sum.
  • A slow task given a fifth of the steps: final success 0.03 under multi-task RL, 0.01 under the periodic sum, 0.70 under OPM, from a start of 0.25. If it never trains: 0.01, 0.00 and 0.14, so protection is per round and partial.

F. Main experimental setup

Model. MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B , a 9.4B dense model with the Qwen3.5-9B architecture, already supervised-fine-tuned. Thinking is on in every domain with one chat template shared by all specialists and arms, so weights stay mergeable; earlier turns’ thinking is kept in agentic domains. The language-model head runs in fp32. The vision tower and multi-token-prediction head are excluded from merges and keep the anchor’s values.

Training repositories are decontaminated against the SWE-bench evaluation sets, and one AIME26 duplicate is removed from DAPO. A held-out suite no arm trains on: MMLU-Pro, GPQA and HLE (the older publicly available release, not comparable to published HLE numbers). Base scores are re-measured in our harnesses, with one fixed open harness per agentic domain for every arm. The knowledge-work judge is a closed-API model, a reproducibility caveat.

Shared RL recipe. slime, run asynchronously with bounded staleness (at most 4 for reasoning; for agentic domains the rollout-to-step time ratio, with the same rule in every arm). GRPO with groups of 16 (8 for agentic domains) : advantage is reward minus the group mean with no standard-deviation normalisation, a global token-mean loss, clipping 0.2 / 0.28, train–inference mismatch masking with IcePop , zero-variance groups dropped, no entropy bonus, no KL penalty. Environment-observation tokens are masked out of the loss, the drift KL and the Fisher.

Budget. Agentic domains: 32 prompts × 8 rollouts per step for 200 steps. Math and instruction following: 32 × 16 for 300 steps. These define the per-domain rollout budget every arm matches. Learning rates are chosen per trainer type (single-domain, multi-task, MOPD) from {1,2,4}×10−6\{1,2,4\}\times10^{-6}{1,2,4}×10−6 on held-out reward, using 15% of the budget on four domains, and frozen before the comparison. Three seeds per arm.

Arms. A1 multi-task RL: per-domain rollout quotas matched to the budget, uniform gradient weights per domain through a ledger rule, deficit scheduling with slow-source replay; a data-proportional mixture as a secondary variant. A2 merge-after: the best of task arithmetic at λ∈{0.4,0.6,0.8,1.0}\lambda\in\{0.4,0.6,0.8,1.0\}λ∈{0.4,0.6,0.8,1.0} chosen on held-out reward, DARE-TA, TIES, the closed form of Liu et al. and a one-shot OPM merge. A3 MOPD: per-token advantage teacher minus student log-probability, clipped to ±5, 30–60 steps, with an outcome-reward variant and a two-round variant; student rollouts count toward the budget. A4 OPM: eight trainers, drift measured on about one rollout in eight, a per-token ceiling, non-blocking rendezvous, the guarded merge (finite-difference logit step 0.01, three CG iterations from the sum, γ\gammaγ on held-out true KL), rollouts in flight kept with per-token importance weights.

Metrics. Per benchmark, the score normalised from base (0) to that domain’s specialist (1); the mean and the worst domain are primary, with 95% confidence intervals over three seeds and several samples per task. Cost from one shared ledger: GPU-hours including teacher scoring and merges, wall-clock, rollouts per domain. Secondary: the held-out suite, a cross-domain matrix (each arm and specialist on every domain), response length, entropy, thinking leakage, tool-call validity, and OPM’s per-rendezvous diagnostics.

G. Secondary findings in detail

Orthogonal is not independent. At 4B, global cosines between task vectors are at most 0.022 and mostly below 0.002, yet the off-diagonal interference index has median 0.122 and maximum 1.78 (Appendix D). Directions along the specialists’ updates carry 5,800 times the Fisher curvature of random directions of the same norm. Whether two domains interfere is a property of their Fishers’ overlap, which cosines do not measure; this is the coupling table of B.2.

Sparsity is a bf16 artefact. On layer-16 tensors of the 4B specialists, task vectors have ∥τ∥/∥θ∥≈7×10−4\|\tau\|/\|\theta\|\approx7\times10^{-4}∥τ∥/∥θ∥≈7×10−4 per layer and a median entry of about 1.1×10−51.1\times10^{-5}1.1×10−5, about 2−112^{-11}2−11 relative to the weights, exactly the rounding step of TF32. In fp32, 99.996% of entries are nonzero. After bf16 rounding only 18% are, the rounded task vector has cosine 0.57 with the true one, and its relative L2 error is 84%. The layer-16 cosines of Wu et al. reproduce exactly (math–science 0.0217, math–code 0.0103), so near-orthogonality is real; apparent sparsity is not. Building the merge from bf16 checkpoints instead of fp32 raises the median off-diagonal interference from 0.122 to 0.14 and the maximum from 1.78 to 2.51.

The bf16 floor. The KL between an fp32 specialist and its own bf16 cast, as a fraction of its drift from the base: math 0.276, science 0.248, code 0.314, IF 0.247, agent 0.403. Deploying the OPM merge in fp32 adds 1.30 ± 0.34 points on the eight-benchmark mean (1.03 on the domain-balanced mean), mostly on AIME, GPQA and LiveCodeBench. Whether fp32 deployment favours the OPM merge specifically is open, because the sum was not evaluated in fp32. Merges, residuals and triggers must be computed in true fp32; perturbations at the 2−112^{-11}2−11 level are invisible to TF32.

KL residual is not reward loss. The sum has the largest residual (1.19 of drift in-sample, up to 3.09 on code) and the best one-shot mean among bf16 merges. By Lemma 2 the return change is the reward-weighted log-ratio plus at most the KL; to first order ρσ2ε\rho\sigma\sqrt{2\varepsilon}ρσ2ε​, with the reward–log-ratio correlation ρ\rhoρ estimated at 0.1–0.3 here. The residual bounds how much of a specialist’s own behaviour is lost, which is the right objective when domains conflict and the wrong one when they help each other.

When the sum beats OPM. In the regime map of B.8, aligned overlap with Cj>0C_j>0Cj​>0 favours the sum. One-shot at 4B, the reasoning domains are in that regime and IF and agent in the low-visibility one, where the sum and the OPM merge tie; so the sum is the best one-shot merge at equal (bf16) precision. The same release also shows the conflicting regime outside the merge: in their evaluation, the IF specialist trained alone lowers BFCL from 63.9 to 54.1, and the agent and code specialists lose about 2 points on AIME25 . Table 6 and Figure 4 measure which regime each of the eight main domains falls in.

The stale metric ties at one shot. A Fisher from base-model rollouts gives a worse residual (0.38 vs 0.31 held-out) but the same benchmark mean (−0.22 ± 0.31). In the toy a metric that was never refreshed failed badly (0.13 against 0.96) because it was used across many rounds. One shot cannot tell the two apart; the main runs log both.

H. Extended related work

The objective and the loop. Distral shares a distilled policy across tasks and regularises each task policy toward it by KL . Divide-and-Conquer RL trains one policy per context, periodically distils them into a central policy on their own trajectories, and resets them to it . That is objective (1) solved by gradient descent at a fixed interval; the barycenter objective is theirs. Policy distillation compresses several task policies into one network . OPM replaces distillation by its closed form in one shared network, and adds the KL trigger and the coupling theory. Co-Evolving Policy Distillation runs per-domain GRPO branches that distil into each other during training and merges them at the end . WARP runs parallel RLHF policies with a moving EMA anchor, merges them by spherical interpolation and re-initialises, for one task and on a fixed schedule .

The merge rule. Fisher-weighted averaging , RegMean’s layer-wise Gram solve and MaTS, which solves the same system with conjugate gradient , are applied once to finished supervised models with diagonal, layer or empirical Fishers, for which the gradient need not lie in the Fisher’s range. FedFish derives a function-space average and applies it each round in supervised federated learning . Liu et al. show that MOPD is Fisher merging to second order; B.7 adds the lossless statement and which Fisher to use. M2A merges a math task vector into a software agent only along the null space of agent-critical activations , which is the intuition of Theorem 1 applied once.

Combining RL domains. Controlled comparisons of mixing, merging and distillation at small scale find them within a few points of each other, with the ordering depending on budget and benchmark ,. Cascade RL trains domains in sequence ,. Frontier reports train specialists and consolidate by on-policy distillation ,,, building on on-policy distillation of language models ,; MiMo-V2.6 runs mixed RL followed by multi-teacher distillation .

Federated and local optimisation. Periodic averaging of local trainers is federated averaging and DiLoCo ,; its bias under heterogeneous clients is client drift, addressed by proximal terms, control variates and normalised averaging ,,. For log-linear policies (M=0M=0M=0) OPM has no drift bias; otherwise lossless rounds still leave a floor proportional to M(1+nκc)2ηKG2M(1+n\kappa_c)^2\eta KG^2M(1+nκc​)2ηKG2 (B.4). Federated natural policy gradient for multi-task RL aggregates natural gradients for a common objective ; the tabular reduction in B.3 shows why the multi-task Fisher, not an average of directions, is needed when domains visit different states. Federated GRPO with plain averaging fell below local-only training under non-IID data . FedKL penalises KL to the global policy . Synchronising when models drift apart rather than on a clock has been used with parameter distance in supervised decentralised training ; we know of no use of trajectory KL to trigger a weight merge.

Policy optimisation. The natural policy gradient and trust-region policy optimisation supply the geometry; the return bound of B.6 is the standard trust-region argument applied to a merge residual. The limitations of the empirical Fisher are why the metric has to be computed on the trainer’s own samples.
